author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Correct a half-screen or offset PS2 post-processing pass
summary: Verify that bloom, blur, depth-of-field, or color grading aligns at native resolution, identify the exact upscale multiplier that displaces it, and apply only a documented coordinate or sprite correction to the affected title.
heroAlt: PCSX2 upscaling diagram showing texture coordinates that can sample outside the intended source area

blocks.text: Find the resolution boundary where the pass moves

Many PS2 post-processes draw a previous framebuffer back onto screen-sized sprites. At native output, the console's sampling can hide small coordinate gaps. Higher internal resolution may expose a shifted source rectangle, an uncovered strip, or an effect applied to only part of the frame. Confirm the content is otherwise correct at native resolution before treating it as an alignment issue.

Skip-draw values copied from a forum can remove the broken pass and make the screenshot look cleaner, but they may also delete lighting, depth-of-field, fog, or later effects. Removal is not correction.

items: A scene where the effect covers a known portion of the image.
Native and upscaled screenshots captured at the same camera and animation moment.
The title serial and revision recorded for patch or GameDB matching.
Default renderer and all manual GS corrections reset.
A clean per-game profile export for rollback.

blocks.text: Map displacement before selecting a correction

items: 1. Cold-boot at native internal resolution and capture the complete post-process boundary.
2. Increase resolution by one multiplier and repeat without changing aspect ratio or filtering.
3. Continue one step at a time until the pass shifts, splits, or leaves an uncovered edge.
4. Return to the first failing multiplier and compare the other hardware API with identical settings.
5. Use software rendering at native output only to confirm the intended composition if the hardware baseline is ambiguous.
6. Consult title- and serial-specific documentation for a half-pixel, sprite-alignment, native-scaling, or texture-offset correction.
7. Apply one documented control, repeat both the first failing and desired multipliers, and inspect 2D overlays.
8. Visit a second effect-heavy area and an FMV before committing the per-game setting.

blocks.text: A correction changes how emulated sprite or texture coordinates map to the larger host target. Because games construct full-screen effects differently, the right value for one executable can shift fonts or break another. Recording the first failing multiplier and serial makes the choice falsifiable instead of turning the graphics profile into a collection of inherited hacks.
The selected correction must cover the intended frame without moving unrelated layers.

items: Bloom, blur, or grading begins and ends at the same boundaries as native output.
No black strip, doubled edge, or untreated half remains during camera movement.
HUD, subtitles, and menu sprites stay aligned.
FMV is not cropped or shifted by the gameplay correction.
The effect remains correct at the chosen multiplier after a cold boot.
The effect disappears entirely: remove skip-draw or disabling controls.
Text shifts while the post-process improves: the coordinate fix is too broad for this title.
Only a different region fails: split profiles by serial and verify the target revision.
Native output is already offset: investigate renderer correctness or the game image before upscaling.

blocks.text: Remove coordinate overrides in reverse order

Disable the single tested correction, restore the last clean internal resolution, and re-import the saved per-game profile if other values changed. Cold-boot native and target checkpoints so both the correct baseline and known failure boundary are documented.
Aspect ratio can imitate a coordinate fault

Stretching 4:3 output to a wider viewport can make a valid effect appear displaced relative to HUD art. Establish the game's original aspect and disable widescreen patches before diagnosing texture-coordinate alignment.
